PullRequest.Title: NES: add applied-then-undone rejected-edit memory mode
PullRequest.Body:
## Summary

Adds a second rejected-edit memory mode, `memory.rejectedEdits: "appliedThenUndone"`, next to the existing `diffWithTags` (#327367).

Instead of a `<|rejected/|>` tag plus an instruction, the rejected suggestion is written into `edit_diff_history` as **ordinary entries**, at the position where the rejection happened: the suggestion is applied and then undone by the developer. Later edits push the pair back like any other history entry.

There is no tag, no instruction, and no system prompt change. The prompt's postscript already says "Avoid undoing or reverting the developer's last change", and this mode relies on that existing behaviour.

```diff
--- src/dialog-form.tsx
+++ src/dialog-form.tsx
@@ -170,1 +170,1 @@
-    isRequired={false}
+    isRequired={true}        <- applied

--- src/dialog-form.tsx
+++ src/dialog-form.tsx
@@ -170,1 +170,1 @@
-    isRequired={true}
+    isRequired={false}       <- undone
```

## Configuration

Everything is controlled through `memory` in the model configuration. With `memory.rejectedEdits` unset (the default), nothing changes: rejections are not recorded into the history, the prompt is unchanged, and a rejection marks the cache as before. Every other option applies only when `rejectedEdits` is set.

| Option | Optional values | Default | Applies to | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `rejectedEdits` | `diffWithTags`, `appliedThenUndone` | unset (off) | - | Turns the memory on and selects how a rejection is written into `edit_diff_history`. `diffWithTags`: one entry with a `<\|rejected/\|>` tag plus an instruction (existing). `appliedThenUndone`: the suggestion applied, then undone, as ordinary entries with no tag and no instruction |
| `rejectedEditsMaxEditsAfter` | number | `4` | both modes | A rejection is used only while at most this many edit-history entries follow it, so older rejections are dropped to save prompt tokens. Consecutive edits to the same line count once |
| `rejectedEditsPlacement` | `inPlace`, `newest` | `inPlace` | both modes | `inPlace`: the rejection stays where it happened and later edits push it back like any other entry. `newest`: it is placed as the newest entries of the history on every request, while it is used |
| `rejectedEditsRepetitions` | number (at least 1) | `1` | `appliedThenUndone` | How many times the applied/undone pair is written |
| `rejectedEditsMaxCount` | number | all recorded rejections | both modes | Only this many of the most recent rejections are used |
| `rejectedEditsCacheScope` | `request`, `edit` | `request` | both modes | What a rejection marks as rejected in the next-edit cache. `request`: every cached suggestion of the same model request, including ones never shown (existing behaviour). `edit`: only the rejected suggestion, so the other suggestions of that response can still be shown |

`appliedThenUndone` additionally uses only rejections in the active document. Like every other history entry, a rejection keeps the line numbers it had when it happened.

Minimal configuration:

```json
"memory": { "rejectedEdits": "appliedThenUndone" }
```

## Running an experiment

Each experiment arm is one model configuration string, set through `chat.advanced.inlineEdits.xtabProvider.modelConfigurationString`. The arms differ only in `memory`; the rest of the configuration stays the same as the control. The memory options are read from the selected model's configuration, so the arm's string must use that model's name.

| Arm | `memory` |
|---|---|
| Control | not set |
| Applied-then-undone, in place | `{ "rejectedEdits": "appliedThenUndone" }` |
| Applied-then-undone, newest | `{ "rejectedEdits": "appliedThenUndone", "rejectedEditsPlacement": "newest" }` |
| Applied-then-undone, in place, cache scope `edit` | `{ "rejectedEdits": "appliedThenUndone", "rejectedEditsCacheScope": "edit" }` |
| Tag (existing mode) | `{ "rejectedEdits": "diffWithTags" }` |

For example, the second arm:

```json
{
  "modelName": "<model name>",
  "promptingStrategy": "<strategy>",
  "includeTagsInCurrentFile": false,
  "memory": { "rejectedEdits": "appliedThenUndone" }
}
```

The value is this object serialized as a string. A version of the extension without this change does not know `appliedThenUndone` or the new options and ignores the whole configuration, so the experiment's version filter must include this change.

## Offline evaluation

Offline evaluation details are in an internal issue: https://github.com/ai-platform-microsoft/aims-tscience-nl2code/issues/3348. In summary:
- Applied-then-undone reduces exact repeats of a rejected suggestion much more than the tag does.
- Suggestions unrelated to the rejection are affected less the further back the rejection is in the history.
- Known risk: when the developer rejected one version of an edit on a line and wants a near-identical version, the model sometimes reproduces the rejected text. We plan to measure this during the flight.

## Changes

- `xtabPromptOptions.ts`:
  - Add `RejectedEditsMemoryMode.AppliedThenUndone` and the options in the table above.
  - `isRejectedEditMemoryEnabled` is now true for either mode.
- `diffHistoryForPrompt.ts`:
  - `selectRejectedEditsForPrompt` applies the conditions above.
  - `getEditDiffHistory` takes the memory options and renders the applied/undone entries, at the rejection's position or as the newest entries. The pair counts as one entry towards `nEntries`. Over-budget rejections are skipped as before.
- `promptCrafting.ts` / `xtabProvider.ts`:
  - Use the selector in both the legacy and global-budget paths.
  - The instruction is only added for `diffWithTags`.
- `nextEditProvider.ts` / `nextEditCache.ts`: with `rejectedEditsCacheScope: "edit"`, a rejection marks only the rejected cache entry.
- Tests:
  - Rendering, and each selection condition.
  - The prompt is unchanged when there is no rejection.
  - Prompt contents and config validation.

## Validation

Validated with unit tests and in a local client build.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The call path is direct: each next-edit request calls `getUserPrompt`, which calls `getEditDiffHistory`, which invokes this renderer for a retained rejection. `vNumber()` checks only `typeof`, JSON model configuration can contain arbitrarily large finite numbers, and both `computeTokens(docDiff)` and the 120K final prompt guard execute only after this allocation. Rejection history itself is bounded to three entries and 3000 characters each, but configured repetition count is unbounded.
Findings.PerformanceResource: temporary arrays and repeated prompt-string bytes
Findings.PerformanceScaling: O(R * S) temporary objects and bytes per next-edit request, where R is the unbounded configured repetition count and S is the applied/undone rejected-diff size (up to roughly twice the retained 3000-character rejection payload, plus headers); up to three retained rejections can trigger this work.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: increased inline-edit latency and CPU/GC pressure, potentially process memory exhaustion
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR there was no repetition option and each rejected edit rendered once, so prompt construction remained bounded by the three-entry/3000-character rejection-history limits.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Applied-then-undone rejection rendering now eagerly creates one full applied/undone string pair per configured repetition before token-budget checks run.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: RIGHT line 211 newly calls `Array.from({ length: repetitions }, ...)`, where `repetitions` comes from the new `memory.rejectedEditsRepetitions` option. The same diff validates that option only with `vNumber()`, and line 70 clamps only the lower bound, not the upper bound.
Findings.Title: Cap repetitions before materializing rejected history
Findings.Impact: With applied-then-undone enabled and at least one retained rejection, a large or accidentally mistyped repetition value makes every subsequent inline-edit request synchronously allocate and scan megabytes or more of throwaway prompt text before rejecting it as over budget. This causes request latency, CPU/GC spikes, and at sufficiently large values can exhaust memory, even though no oversized prompt can be sent.
Findings.Evidence: `repetitions` is derived as `Math.max(1, Math.floor(memory?.rejectedEditsRepetitions ?? 1))` without a maximum. This line allocates an array of that length, creates a full interpolated pair for every element, and joins all pairs. Only after it returns does `getEditDiffHistory` call `computeTokens(docDiff)` and compare against `maxTokens`; the provider's 120K-character hard limit is later still. The model configuration parser accepts any JSON number because `vNumber()` performs only a `typeof` check.
Findings.Recommendation: Validate `rejectedEditsRepetitions` as a small bounded integer and enforce that bound again at rendering; preferably compute one pair's token/character cost and stop before materializing repetitions that cannot fit the remaining history budget.

Scenarios.Scenario: Request an inline next edit after rejecting a suggestion, with rejected-edit memory enabled
Scenarios.CriticalPath: On a cache miss, language context and neighbor snippets are awaited, then `getUserPrompt` synchronously selects and renders rejection history, computes token counts, applies the final character guard, debounces, and only then starts the model request. The new repetition allocation is therefore on the critical path and is not cancellable while it is executing.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Gather registered language-context items and neighbor-file snippets
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one language-context gather and one neighbor-snippet gather per next-edit request when enabled; provider/snippet cardinality is unchanged by the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same context gathers occurred before this PR.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Both gathers are awaited before synchronous prompt rendering; the new allocation delays progress after they complete.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send the completed prompt to the selected model with `endpoint.makeChatRequest2`
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One model request per issued next-edit fetch after existing request reuse/debounce; oversized prompts return before this boundary.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: One model request used the bounded single rendering of each rejection; the network boundary and its cardinality are unchanged.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The model request cannot start until prompt rendering and guards finish. Large repetition values can spend substantial CPU/memory and then return `PromptTooLarge` without ever reaching the network.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Rejected history is effectively bounded to 3 entries of at most 3000 retained characters each and edit history to 50 entries. Selection work is at most 3x50 comparisons per pass, but rendered bytes scale linearly with the newly configured `rejectedEditsRepetitions`, which has no upper bound; global-budget requests select twice but reuse the rendered cascade.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each next-edit request constructs its own prompt synchronously. Existing request reuse/cancellation may suppress some duplicate fetches, but there is no shared limiter or cancellation checkpoint inside the new repeated-string construction, so concurrent/speculative cache misses can each pay the allocation independently.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Rejected and edit histories are in-memory snapshots; rendered rejection text is not cached and is rebuilt on each request. A warm next-edit cache can bypass the model-request path entirely, but any cache miss after a rejection reruns prompt construction. There is no negative prompt-render cache or coalescing introduced by this diff.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: validation accepts any JSON number, rendering eagerly allocates all repetitions, and token/final-size checks occur only afterward on every cache-miss prompt path.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Default repetition is 1, so affected prevalence depends on an explicit local or experiment model configuration. The exact pause/OOM threshold depends on rejection size and runtime memory, but accidental values in the hundreds or thousands already create repeated megabyte-scale temporary strings, while JSON permits much larger finite values.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable medium-severity regression: the new unbounded repetition value controls synchronous pre-budget allocation and scanning on the inline-edit critical path.

Scenarios.Scenario: Reject one edit from a multi-edit model response with `rejectedEditsCacheScope: edit`
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The rejection handler records the bounded rejection history and directly flags the displayed `CachedEdit`; subsequent sibling suggestions may remain cache hits. No subprocess, IPC, filesystem, database, or network operation is added to the rejection callback.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: One displayed cache entry is mutated. Under the prior/default request scope, rejection scans the shared cache and flags entries sharing the request ID; cache cardinality and lifetime are unchanged.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The callback is synchronous and performs one object mutation in edit scope; no new task, queue, fan-out, or boundary concurrency is created.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The new edit scope preserves positive sibling cache entries from the same response, while request scope keeps prior invalidation behavior. Cache keys, eviction, cold misses, and request coalescing are unchanged by the diff.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the changed branch either marks one supplied entry or executes the pre-existing request-ID scan.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The cache-hit benefit depends on multi-edit response usage, but no adverse performance mechanism is present.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance regression; edit scope reduces invalidation work and can avoid later model cache misses.

Scenarios.Scenario: Request an inline edit with rejection memory disabled, or enabled with no retained rejection
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The selector returns immediately when disabled, or scans at most the three-entry rejection list when enabled; the existing context gathering, prompt construction, debounce, and single model network request remain the critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send the next-edit prompt to the model with `endpoint.makeChatRequest2`
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One request per issued cache-miss fetch, unchanged by the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same model call occurred with the same prompt when no rejection was present.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Remains after context gathering, prompt construction, guards, and debounce; no changed work is material when rejection memory is disabled or empty.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Zero rejected entries in the common no-rejection case; edit history remains bounded at 50.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: No new work is scheduled and no concurrency or fan-out changes occur.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The generated prompt is unchanged when no rejection exists. Existing next-edit cache cold/warm behavior and model-request reuse are unaffected.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the disabled branch returns an empty array immediately and tests establish byte-identical prompt output when enabled but empty.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: None material; added selector overhead is constant/near-zero under this input and bounded under all retained-history inputs.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression for the default configuration or empty rejection history.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 10 changed files. Traced prompt construction, bounded edit/rejection history, cache rejection handling, context gathering, final prompt guards, and the model network boundary. Submitted one medium-severity serialization/allocation finding for unbounded eager repetition before budget checks; bounded selection work and cache-scope changes do not introduce additional regressions.
